entries.name: Brava Island Arabica — Volcanic Ridge Altitude Coffee, Most Remote Cape Verde Cultivation, Atlantic Isolation Single-Island Terroir, PCT Atlantic Island Coffee Heritage
entries.sub_tradition: single-origin Arabica — volcanic island, natural-process, altitude-grown
entries.region: Cape Verde — Brava Island (Arabica Altitude Coffee, Volcanic Ridge, Atlantic Isolation, Fogo Island Cross-Pollination)
entries.terroir_origin: Brava is the smallest inhabited island of the Cape Verde archipelago and the most remote — a 65km² volcanic cone rising from the Atlantic at 10°N latitude, accessible only by the infrequent inter-island ferry from Fogo (the neighbouring volcanic island known for its Pico do Fogo active volcano and the Santiago Grogue rum tradition documented in pct_40). The island's primary settlement is Nova Sintra (population approximately 6,000), situated at 520–550m above sea level on the rim of the island's central volcanic crater-highland. The coffee cultivation on Brava is confined to the fertile volcanic ridge above Nova Sintra at 400–700m altitude, where the northeast trade winds provide consistent cooling and the volcanic basalt-lapilli soils (the same volcanic geology as Fogo Island, 30km to the northeast) provide the iron-rich, porous substrate that concentrates mineral compounds in the cherry. Annual rainfall at the Nova Sintra ridge is 250–400mm — at the lower boundary of adequate coffee cultivation and significantly less than the Ethiopian or Colombian growing regions — supplemented by the Atlantic fog-drip that the trade winds drive into the highlands for approximately 6–8 months of the year. The fog-drip hydration during the dry season is the critical water source for the Brava coffee cultivation; without it, the island's rainfall would be insufficient to maintain the Arabica trees in the volcanic basalt substrate. The geographic isolation — Brava is separated from the nearest major landmass (Senegal) by 450km of open Atlantic — has produced a genetically isolated population of Coffea arabica that has evolved over three centuries without cross-pollination from mainland or non-archipelago varieties, producing a phenotypically distinct Brava ecotype with smaller cherry, denser bean, and lower natural caffeine compared to continental Arabica benchmarks.
entries.production_technique: Brava Island coffee production is entirely subsistence-scale and family-managed, with no industrial processing infrastructure present on the island. The cultivation follows a traditional agroforestry model — the coffee trees grow beneath the shade of indigenous cape gooseberry, papaya, and banana trees at 400–700m altitude, providing natural shade-grown conditions that slow cherry development and increase cup complexity. Harvesting is by selective hand-picking at full red or yellow cherry maturity (the Brava ecotype produces both red and yellow cherry variants from the same lineage), typically in November–February. Processing: Brava uses the natural (dry) process exclusively — the infrastructure for washed processing (adequate water, raised drying beds, central processing mills) is not available on the island. The cherries are dried in whole-fruit on simple ground-level drying mats or on concrete patios in Nova Sintra for 4–6 weeks, depending on cloud cover and trade wind intensity. The natural processing under Atlantic trade wind conditions — different from the still, hot air of Ethiopian Harrar or Yirgacheffe natural processing — produces a specific drying dynamic: the trade wind evaporation prevents the fermentation temperatures from reaching the high levels that produce the "winey" overfermented character sometimes found in poorly managed Ethiopian natural processing, while still allowing the full development of the stone fruit and dried berry flavor compounds from the natural sugar migration from cherry mucilage into the bean. Milling is performed with simple hand-operated or small motorised pulpers transported to the island from Praia (Santiago Island). No grading by density or screen size is typically performed for domestic consumption. The coffee is roasted locally by the producers themselves on simple drum roasters or open-fire clay pot roasters, producing a full-city to dark roast that is the Cape Verde domestic preference — the same dark roast tradition that defines the grogue cafezinho service culture of the archipelago.

cross_tradition_parallels.tradition: coffee — Fogo Island Cape Verde (volcanic, PCT Atlantic sibling)
cross_tradition_parallels.beverage: Fogo Island Arabica — Pico do Fogo Volcanic Terroir, Atlantic Island Natural Process
cross_tradition_parallels.connection: Brava and Fogo Island coffee cultivation are the two surviving expressions of the same Portuguese colonial Arabica introduction into the Cape Verde archipelago that began in the 17th century. Both islands share identical volcanic geology (the Fogo volcanic system produced both islands through the same Atlantic hotspot geological event), identical trade wind exposure, and essentially the same Arabica ecotype — the genetic isolation of each island has produced measurable phenotypic divergence over three centuries, but the two ecotypes are more similar to each other than to any continental Arabica. The difference is the volcanic profile: Fogo coffee grows on the active Pico do Fogo (2,829m) and benefits from more recent volcanic mineral inputs; Brava coffee grows on the older, dormant volcanic ridge with more weathered basalt producing a mellower mineral character. Both represent the same PCT Atlantic island coffee heritage but from contrasting volcanic terroir ages.

cross_tradition_parallels.tradition: coffee — São Tomé and Príncipe equatorial island (Atlantic, volcanic, shade-grown)
cross_tradition_parallels.beverage: São Tomé Arabica — Roça System, Biosphere Reserve, Colonial Estate Heritage
cross_tradition_parallels.connection: Brava Island coffee and São Tomé coffee are the two Atlantic island volcanic single-origin coffees of the Portuguese colonial archipelago system — both established through Portuguese colonial agricultural introduction of Arabica to volcanic Atlantic islands in the 17th–18th centuries; both characterised by geographic isolation that has produced genetically distinct ecotypes; both using natural processing exclusively due to limited processing infrastructure. The terroir divergence is altitude and latitude: São Tomé grows at 0°N (equatorial) with full tropical humidity at 300–800m; Brava grows at 14°N (subtropical Atlantic) with trade-wind-driven aridity at 400–700m. Both are among the world's smallest coffee-producing territories by volume and among the least known internationally despite their historical significance as the original Portuguese Atlantic island coffee agricultural heritage.

sensory_profile.appearance: The green bean: small to medium sized (screen 14–16), dense, dark green-grey with a characteristic matte finish from the natural processing — the dried mucilage coating gives the parchment-removed bean a slightly rougher surface texture than washed-process beans of the same origin; the roasted bean: achieves a very dark surface sheen when taken to the full-city dark roast typical in Cape Verde domestic use, with visible oil on the surface indicating second-crack roast completion.
sensory_profile.nose: At the standard Cape Verde dark roast: intense dark roast aromatics dominate — dark chocolate, roasted nuts, and the characteristic "peaty" smoke of dark-roasted volcanic island coffee from the mineral richness of the basalt substrate; beneath, dried stone fruit (dried fig, prune) from the natural processing; the Atlantic trade wind drying has suppressed the heavy fermentation character of less controlled natural process coffees, producing a cleaner stone-fruit aromatic than the winey overripe profile of poorly managed Ethiopian naturals. At a lighter roast (filter-appropriate medium roast) if accessible: the volcanic mineral character — a saline, iron-rich, almost oceanic mineral note — becomes the dominant aromatic signature, with dried berry, brown sugar, and the characteristic Cape Verde earthiness of the basalt-lapilli soil.
sensory_profile.palate: Full body from the dense natural-process bean and the dark roast development; the entry is immediately defined by the dark chocolate and roast nut register; the mid-palate develops the dried stone fruit and brown sugar sweetness from the natural processing; the volcanic mineral character from the Brava basalt substrate provides a saline dryness at the finish that distinguishes this from continental natural-process coffees — the Atlantic island mineral signature is unmistakable in blind tasting for those familiar with the Fogo Island parallel; the finish is long (25–40 seconds) with dark chocolate and a persistent mineral-saline note; acidity is low (pH 5.0–5.4 in cup) due to the natural processing and the dark roast level; body is full and coating.
sensory_profile.conclusion: The most isolated coffee terroir on the Portuguese colonial trade network — a three-century-old Arabica ecotype grown on Atlantic volcanic basalt by smallholder families in conditions that approach the limits of viable coffee cultivation, producing a mineral-dense cup that is available in quantities too small for commercial global distribution.

quality_hierarchy.criteria: Brava Island single-origin Arabica from identified ridge smallholders above 600m altitude, natural processed and dried on raised beds under consistent trade wind conditions, milled and exported with verifiable origin documentation; available only through specialist Cape Verde importers or direct-from-island sourcing; the international rarity and historical significance add value beyond the intrinsic cup quality; SCA cupping score estimated at 83–86 for a well-prepared natural-process Brava expression.
quality_hierarchy.markers: Identified ridge origin above 600m; natural process; trade-wind dried; Atlantic volcanic mineral profile; small bean screen 14–15; dense green bean.

quality_hierarchy.criteria: Brava Island domestic production available through Cape Verde archipelago retail and the limited island-to-island trade network; natural process; standard dark roast appropriate for the domestic market; consistent origin but without the altitude selection or raised-bed drying of the Reserve tier; the real and accessible Brava coffee experience for visitors to Nova Sintra.
quality_hierarchy.markers: Island origin confirmed; natural process; dark roast; available in Brava domestic market and Cape Verde tourist retail.

quality_hierarchy.criteria: Cape Verde archipelago blended coffee (primarily Fogo Island with Brava, Santo Antão, and imported blending coffee) available in Praia and Mindelo supermarkets under commercial Cape Verde labels; competent dark roast commercial blend without single-island terroir integrity; the everyday Cape Verde domestic coffee.
quality_hierarchy.markers: Multi-island blend; Fogo dominant; commercial Cape Verde label; standard dark roast; no single-origin documentation.

quality_hierarchy.criteria: Imported commercial coffee (Nescafé, Delta, Jacobs) that dominates Cape Verde urban retail — the same industrial coffee available throughout the Portuguese-speaking world without any volcanic island terroir connection; the entry-level category by volume.
quality_hierarchy.markers: Industrial roast; imported; no Cape Verde origin; standard commercial espresso or instant profile.

service_intelligence.temperature: At the traditional Cape Verde domestic dark roast: espresso extraction (93°C, 25-second pull, 7g dose per 30ml cup) in the Portuguese café tradition that dominates Cape Verde café culture — the bica (single espresso) format identical to Lisbon café service. At lighter roast for single-origin specialty use: pour-over V60 or Aeropress at 90–92°C to preserve the volcanic mineral character and stone-fruit natural processing aromatics that the dark roast suppresses. The traditional Cape Verde service is always hot and strong; cold brew is not part of the cultural tradition.
service_intelligence.vessel: Traditional service: a small ceramic demitasse (60–80ml) in the Portuguese bica style, with sugar alongside in a small bowl — the Cape Verde domestic coffee service follows the Lisbon pasteleria model directly (the PCT transmission in beverage service convention is completely intact in Brava: the same glass and the same sugar service as Lisbon, 3,000km to the northeast). For specialty programme use at lighter roast: a 250ml ceramic pour-over cup or V60 server, served without sugar to demonstrate the volcanic mineral character. Present with a card describing the Brava Island geography (65km², 6,000 people, accessible by ferry only, 400km from Africa) — the story of the origin is the essential service element for international coffee professionals encountering this origin for the first time.
service_intelligence.technique: Espresso for domestic tradition; V60 or Aeropress at 90–92°C for specialty single-origin evaluation. Always describe the Fogo Island parallel and the Atlantic isolation terroir context.
service_intelligence.programme_position: PCT Atlantic island coffee flight: Brava alongside Fogo Island (already in system, pct_40), São Tomé, and potentially Madeira (limited production) for a Portuguese colonial Atlantic archipelago coffee heritage flight — the rarest origin tasting in the PCT system.
service_intelligence.verbal_presentation: The most isolated coffee on the Portuguese trade network. Brava Island. Accessible only by ferry from Fogo. Grown on the same volcanic ridge for three centuries. The bean is small and dense because the Atlantic wind and volcanic rock allow almost nothing else. You may never find this coffee twice.

purveyor_intelligence.benchmark_producer: Brava Island smallholder families above Nova Sintra — no single benchmark commercial producer exists; the closest to a reference is the INIDA-supported (Cape Verde National Agriculture Research Institute) smallholder cooperative programme on Brava that periodically exports small lots to European specialty coffee buyers. Fogo Organic Coffee cooperative (the pct_40 reference producer) sometimes blends or co-exports Brava lots with their Fogo production.

purveyor_intelligence.availability_notes: Brava Island coffee is one of the rarest commercial single-origin coffees in the world by production volume. It appears at international specialty coffee auctions only sporadically and in quantities of under 1,000kg per lot. For professional programme buyers, the most reliable route is through the INIDA Cape Verde agricultural institute or through direct contact with Fogo Island specialty producers who sometimes co-export Brava lots. Green bean price is high due to scarcity: USD $12–20 per kg green bean when available internationally.

entries.trail_note: Brava Island coffee completes the Cape Verde PCT node with the coffee dimension to complement the grogue (sugarcane rum) and the Portuguese café culture already documented. The three Portuguese Atlantic island coffee origins — Brava, Fogo (pct_40), and São Tomé (pct_83) — together form the complete arc of Portuguese colonial agricultural heritage in the tropical Atlantic, all three derived from the same Arabica introduction through the Portuguese colonial trade network into volcanic island environments that have produced genetically distinct ecotypes over three centuries of Atlantic isolation.

food_pairings.dish: Bolo de mel (Cape Verde molasses cake — Portuguese colonial dark sugar cake tradition)
food_pairings.rationale: The dark roast dark chocolate and caramel character of Brava Island espresso bridges directly to the molasses-sweetened dark cake of Cape Verde bolo de mel — both derived from the colonial sugar trade that the PCT established through Cape Verde as a sugar transit point; the cake sweetness cuts the coffee bitterness while the dark sugar amplifies the roast aromatic.

food_pairings.dish: Queijo de cabra fresco (fresh Cape Verde goat's dairy product, light, slightly salted)
food_pairings.rationale: The volcanic mineral-saline character of Brava coffee at lighter roast provides a deliberate mineral contrast to the clean lactic freshness of Cape Verde fresh goat dairy — both express the Atlantic island terroir (the goats graze the volcanic basalt ridge where the coffee grows) through complementary mineral registers that highlight the volcanic terroir from two production paths.
